summary: Describes a Transport Model that carries SNMP over the Secure Shell (SSH) protocol, giving encrypted and authenticated management traffic. It also defines MIB objects to monitor and manage this model.

eli5.summary: SNMP messages are like notes about network devices. This puts the notes inside a locked SSH box while they travel.

subtitle: How SNMP management traffic can ride inside an SSH session, reusing the SSH logins and keys operators already have.

tldr.problem: SNMPv3's own User-based Security Model needs its own user and key-management setup, and operators reported that having to deploy it was a reason for not deploying SNMPv3.
tldr.mechanism: The Secure Shell Transport Model (SSHTM) sends SNMP messages through an SSH session, using an SSH subsystem named "snmp", and takes the authenticated SSH user name as the identity for SNMP access control.
tldr.outcome: SNMP can reuse the commonly deployed SSH security infrastructure, always with authentication, integrity and encryption (authPriv). The RFC is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted or updated.

today: RFC 5592 is a Proposed Standard, published in June 2009, and the metadata for this document lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It works together with the Transport Subsystem in RFC 5590 and the Transport Security Model in RFC 5591.

sections.title: Why Run SNMP Over SSH
sections.content:
SNMPv3 added security to the Simple Network Management Protocol. Its User-based Security Model (USM, RFC 3414) was built to be independent of other security infrastructure, so it could work even in a broken network. The price is a separate user and key-management system. Operators reported that having to deploy another one was a reason for not deploying SNMPv3.

This RFC defines a Transport Model that uses the Secure Shell security infrastructure instead. It is called the Secure Shell Transport Model (SSHTM) and plugs into the SNMP Transport Subsystem from RFC 5590. The RFC also notes that SSH is the approach commonly used for command line interfaces, so one approach can cover SNMPv3 and the CLI.

Two design constraints stand out. In times of network stress, the transport and its security SHOULD NOT depend on other network services such as NTP or AAA protocols. And a Transport Model SHOULD NOT require changes to the SNMP architecture or to the underlying security protocol.
sections.eli5: Normally SNMP needs its own set of passwords and keys, which is a lot of extra work. This idea lets it borrow the passwords and keys that people already use for SSH.

sections.title: Where SSHTM Fits
sections.content:
SSH has three main parts: the Transport Layer Protocol (RFC 4253) gives server authentication, confidentiality and integrity; the User Authentication Protocol (RFC 4252) authenticates the client-side principal; and the Connection Protocol (RFC 4254) splits the encrypted tunnel into logical channels.

SSHTM sits between the SSH transport layer and the SNMP Message Dispatcher. The sending side hands unencrypted messages from the Dispatcher to SSH to be encrypted. The receiving side takes decrypted messages from SSH and passes them up. Several SNMP messages MAY travel through the same channel.

The model also translates between SSH-specific security parameters and the model-independent parameters SNMP uses. For incoming messages it records the authenticated identity and related data in a cache referenced by tmStateReference and passes it along with the message to the Dispatcher.
sections.eli5: SSHTM is a mail clerk between SNMP and SSH. It takes a note from SNMP, puts it in the locked SSH box, and on the other end opens the box and hands the note to the next SNMP clerk.

sections.title: Security Capabilities and Identity
sections.content:
SSHTM is meant to counter the threats named in the SNMP architecture. SSH signs each packet, so modification is detected. It verifies the SSH server's identity and the client's identity, protects against reordering and replay within a session by using sequence numbers and integrity checks, and encrypts traffic so it is not disclosed to eavesdroppers. Keys are generated afresh for each session, which guards against replay across sessions.

Any SSH user-authentication method should work, including publickey, password, hostbased and keyboard-interactive. The none method is NOT RECOMMENDED. A password can be handed to a service such as RADIUS for validation, though the RFC warns that this requires the password to be available as cleartext on the device doing the checking.

The authenticated SSH user name becomes the tmSecurityName. It MUST stay constant for all traffic in a session, and messages MUST NOT be sent through an existing SSH session that was set up with a different one. Both sides need an identity: on the server it is the SSH user name, on the client it comes from the application, possibly from SNMP-TARGET-MIB configuration.
sections.eli5: SSH checks who you are before letting you in, just like a doorman checking a name on a list. Whatever name it confirms is the name SNMP uses when deciding what you are allowed to see.

sections.title: Always Full Protection
sections.content:
SNMP defines three security levels: noAuthNoPriv, authNoPriv and authPriv. SSHTM cannot test whether the underlying SSH connection provides authentication or privacy, so it trusts that the connection is configured properly. A compliant implementation MUST use an SSH connection that provides authentication, data integrity and encryption at the highest level, authPriv.

In practice that means a message requested with noAuthNoPriv or authNoPriv is still sent with authPriv-level protection. Incoming messages are recorded with tmTransportSecurityLevel set to authPriv.
sections.eli5: Even if SNMP says a note is not secret, SSH still puts it in the strongest locked box. Every note gets the best protection.

sections.title: Opening, Using and Closing a Session
sections.content:
When an SNMP application such as a command generator or notification originator needs to send a message, the model looks for an existing SSH session matching the transport address and security name. If there is none, it calls openSession(). If tmSameSecurity is true and no matching session exists, the message is dropped and the snmpSshtmSessionNoSessions counter is incremented.

Opening a session goes in steps. The client makes an SSH transport connection, authenticates the server (usually by checking a stored pair of transport address and server host public key), and exchanges keys. Next it authenticates the principal. If the address has a user@ prefix, that user name is used; otherwise the tmSecurityName is used. Then it invokes the ssh-connection service and requests a channel of type session, and finally starts snmp as an SSH subsystem. A failure at any step closes the connection and increments a matching counter.

To make SNMP traffic easy to identify and filter, servers MUST default to offering the snmp subsystem when the session uses the IANA-assigned TCP ports 5161 and 5162, and SHOULD be configurable to allow it on other ports. Closing a session is left to the implementation to decide when; it increments a counter and has SSH close the session.
sections.eli5: To send a note, SNMP first knocks on the other device's door, proves who it is, checks who is behind the door, and asks for the "snmp" room. Only then does it pass the note through.

sections.title: The SNMP-SSH-TM-MIB
sections.content:
The RFC defines a MIB module, SNMP-SSH-TM-MIB, that lets operators monitor the model. It defines the snmpSSHDomain transport domain identity, a textual convention called SnmpSSHAddress and eight read-only Counter32 counters for sessions. No object is read-write or read-create.

The SnmpSSHAddress format echoes familiar SSH notation: an optional user name and @, then a host name or IP address, a colon and a decimal port number. IPv6 addresses go in square brackets. An SNMP entity using this domain must be able to accept messages up to and including 8192 octets.

The counters track session opens, closes, open errors, user-authentication failures, channel-open failures, subsystem failures, outgoing messages dropped because the same session was gone, and messages dropped because of an invalid cache.
sections.eli5: The MIB is a scoreboard. It counts how often sessions opened, closed or failed, so people can see whether things are going well.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
SSHTM relies on SSH mutual authentication, key binding, confidentiality and integrity. It cannot check that server authentication actually happened, so it trusts that deployers configured it properly. Several settings are therefore forbidden: SSH MUST NOT be used with the none userauth method, MUST NOT have confidentiality or integrity turned off, MUST NOT use the none MAC algorithm, and MUST NOT skip public-key verification of the server. Skipping that verification would leave a client open to an attacker in the middle, and passwords sent after it would be exposed.

Notifications are authorized before the connection is made, so the credentials presented by a notification receiver MUST match what is expected for that address and be cryptographically verified. The RFC also points out that SSH uses asymmetric keys, unlike USM, so keys differ on the two sides and each side must verify the other's key.

With SNMPv1 and SNMPv2c messages, access control still comes from the message contents, not from the authenticated SSH identity. The RFC says that deploying SNMP versions before SNMPv3 is NOT RECOMMENDED.
sections.eli5: The rules say never to turn off the locks or skip checking who is on the other end. A strong lock does not help if you hand your note to the wrong person.

sections.title: Operational Considerations
sections.content:
SSHTM will likely not work when remote CLI access has stopped working, since it assumes TCP and IP work between the nodes. Where management access must be very reliable, the RFC suggests mitigations such as dedicated management-only networks, point-to-point links and alternate protocols or transports. If AAA services are used, operators should also configure local authentication such as local passwords so SNMP keeps working during network stress.

SSH session setup needs CPU-intensive calculations to establish a session key, so short-lived sessions are expensive compared with USM. SSH has no session-resumption feature like TLS, so SNMP applications should keep SSH sessions for longer periods. Internetworking devices are often not configured as SSH clients, so sending notifications requires configuring them with client credentials and a way to authenticate the server.

SSHTM MUST be used with a Security Model that knows how to process a tmStateReference, such as the Transport Security Model in RFC 5591.
sections.eli5: Locked boxes take time to set up, so it is better to keep one open for a long chat than to make a new one for every note. And if the road to the other device is blocked, the box cannot get through.

items.title: Open errors
items.text: Transport connection or server authentication failed.

items.title: User auth failures
items.text: The client could not authenticate the principal.

items.title: Channel failures
items.text: The channel could not be opened.

items.title: Subsystem failures
items.text: The snmp subsystem could not be reached.

items.title: Dropped messages
items.text: Session gone, or the tmStateReference cache was invalid.
